checkpoints: HMAC signatures are computed over raw bytes, not over JSON semantics — the algorithm has no concept of "the same data," so any re-serialization that changes whitespace, indentation, or key order produces a completely different signature even though the parsed object is logically identical.

On the sender side, `JSON.stringify(payload)` is used to compute the signature, but a later "reformat" step runs `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body), null, 2)` before the actual HTTP POST — this produces a second, differently-formatted string, so the bytes that get signed are not the bytes that actually go out over the wire.

On the receiver side, the framework's body parser (e.g. Nest's default JSON parser) has already parsed the incoming request into an object before the handler runs, discarding the original wire bytes; re-stringifying that parsed object with `JSON.stringify(req.body)` yields yet a third, independently-formatted byte sequence rather than what the client actually sent.

Because the sender signs one byte sequence, sends a second, and the receiver reconstructs and signs a third, the two computed HMACs can never match regardless of whether the shared secret is correct — the 401 "signature mismatch" is a serialization bug, not an authentication or secret-mismatch bug.
The correct fix on the sender is to remove the reformat step entirely and transmit the exact same string that was signed, so no re-serialization happens between signing and sending.

The correct fix on the receiver is to capture the raw, unmodified request body before any JSON parsing occurs (e.g. enabling `rawBody: true` when bootstrapping the Nest app and reading `req.rawBody`) and compute the HMAC over those literal bytes instead of re-stringifying the already-parsed `req.body`.

"Logically equal JSON" (same keys and values) and "byte-identical payload" (the exact same byte sequence) are distinct properties, and only byte-identical payloads produce matching HMAC signatures — any middleware, proxy, or serializer that parses and re-emits the body between the signing step and the verification step breaks this guarantee.

Fixing the bug should be verified end-to-end by re-sending a webhook request and confirming the receiver now returns 200 instead of 401, and further confirmed by diffing the exact bytes the sender signed against the exact raw bytes the receiver read to prove byte-for-byte identity rather than just visual similarity.
